x.A: Transfer Acceleration sends uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge location over the AWS backbone, and multipart upload parallelizes the 500 GB transfers. Data lands directly in the one destination bucket with nothing extra to run.
x.B: Uploading to a regional bucket and then using Cross-Region Replication adds a second hop and a cleanup step for every site. It is slower and more complex than uploading straight to the destination.
x.C: Snowball Edge is a physical shipping process. Daily jobs for sites that already have fast internet add days of delay and heavy operational work, and it also needs CRR.
x.D: Staging on EC2 and EBS, then copying snapshots and restoring them in another Region, is a large amount of custom plumbing and still does not put the data in S3 quickly.

x.A: Redshift would require loading the JSON into a cluster and managing it. That is too much setup for simple on-demand queries.
x.B: Moving the logs into CloudWatch Logs changes the existing architecture, and it is not the natural tool for ad hoc SQL over data already in S3.
x.C: Athena is serverless and queries JSON in S3 directly with standard SQL, billed per query. It needs no data movement or infrastructure, so it is the lowest overhead.
x.D: Glue plus a transient EMR Spark cluster works, but launching and managing clusters is far more operational work than Athena.

x.A: The aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key allows any principal from any account in the organization. New accounts are covered automatically, so there is nothing to maintain.
x.B: PrincipalOrgPaths targets specific OUs, so you would need to create and maintain OUs and paths per department. That is unnecessary work when you want the whole organization.
x.C: Watching CloudTrail account events and editing the bucket policy each time is a manual, reactive process with a lot of ongoing work.
x.D: Tagging every user and matching on aws:PrincipalTag requires continuous tag administration and does not tie access to the organization.

x.A: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 adds a route-table target that keeps S3 traffic on the AWS network with no internet gateway or NAT, and it has no additional charge.
x.B: Streaming to CloudWatch Logs and exporting to S3 does not give the instance private access to the bucket. It is a different logging workflow.
x.C: An instance profile grants permissions but does not change the network path, so the instance would still need internet access to reach S3.
x.D: API Gateway private link is for exposing private services to API clients, not for reaching S3 privately from an instance.

x.A: Copying data between the two EBS volumes only syncs a snapshot in time. New uploads would diverge again immediately, and it must be repeated constantly.
x.B: An ALB cannot know which server holds a particular user's documents. Pinning users to one server also hurts availability and does not solve the split data.
x.C: EFS is a shared file system that multiple instances in multiple AZs mount at once, so every server sees all documents. Copying the existing data and saving new uploads there fixes the problem.
x.D: An ALB sends each request to one target. It cannot fan a request out to both servers and merge the answers.

x.A: Copying 70 TB over the internet with the CLI would take a very long time and consume a lot of bandwidth, which the question says to minimize.
x.B: Snowball Edge moves the data offline by shipping a device, so it is fast for 70 TB and uses almost no network bandwidth. AWS imports it into S3 when the device is returned.
x.C: S3 File Gateway still pushes all 70 TB over the network, which is slow and uses bandwidth. The public endpoint doesn't help.
x.D: Direct Connect takes weeks to provision and still sends all the data over the network, so it is slower and costlier than shipping a device.

x.A: Kinesis Data Analytics processes streaming data with SQL or Flink. It is not a message store that dozens of consumers read from, so it does not decouple the system.
x.B: Scaling EC2 on CPU only scales the ingestion tier. The consumers remain tightly coupled to it and nothing buffers the messages.
x.C: A single Kinesis shard accepts only about 1,000 records per second, far below 100,000 per second. Routing through DynamoDB also adds a needless hop.
x.D: SNS fan-out to multiple SQS queues decouples the producer from every consumer, and each consumer reads at its own pace. Both services scale to very high throughput.

x.A: The SQS queue and worker group are right, but scheduled scaling follows a fixed timetable and cannot react to unpredictable variable workloads.
x.B: Jobs go into an SQS queue so the primary server is no longer a single point of failure, and the Auto Scaling group scales on queue size so capacity tracks the workload.
x.C: This keeps the primary server as a bottleneck and single point of failure. CloudTrail is an audit log, not a destination for jobs.
x.D: This also keeps the primary coordinator, and EventBridge is an event router, not a durable job queue. Scaling the workers by their own load does not reflect pending work.

x.A: DataSync copies data to AWS but does not give users a local SMB share with a cache, and it does not manage the lifecycle of the files.
x.B: An S3 File Gateway exposes an SMB share on premises and keeps recently used files in a local cache for low latency. The data itself lives in S3, so capacity is effectively unlimited, and a lifecycle policy moves older files to Glacier Deep Archive.
x.C: FSx for Windows File Server provides a file system in AWS, but it does not extend on-premises storage with a local cache, and it has no built-in tiering of old files to archive storage.
x.D: A utility on every user's computer does not provide a shared SMB file server, and access to the data would no longer be low latency.

x.A: SNS delivers messages to subscribers but does not guarantee the order in which orders are processed.
x.B: An SQS FIFO queue preserves order and provides exactly-once processing, and it can trigger a Lambda function to process each order.
x.C: An authorizer is for authentication and authorization. It cannot serialize order processing, and blocking requests would throttle users.
x.D: A standard SQS queue gives best-effort ordering only, so messages can arrive out of order.

x.A: Secrets Manager stores credentials centrally and has built-in automatic rotation for Aurora, so the application can fetch them at runtime. This removes the manual credential work.
x.B: Parameter Store can hold secure strings, but it has no native automatic rotation, so you would build rotation yourself.
x.C: Storing a credentials file in encrypted S3 only moves the file. Rotation is still manual and the application must be changed to read from S3.
x.D: Putting the file on an encrypted EBS volume is no different from the local file today. There is no rotation and each instance needs its own copy.

x.A: One CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket and the ALB as origins caches static content at the edge and speeds up dynamic content over the AWS backbone. Route 53 aliases the domain to it.
x.B: Global Accelerator cannot use an S3 bucket as an endpoint, so this design is not valid.
x.C: Global Accelerator in front of CloudFront and the ALB is not a valid or useful combination, and CloudFront already accelerates both origins. It adds cost and complexity.
x.D: This also puts S3 behind Global Accelerator, which is unsupported, and splitting into two domain names makes the application harder to use.

x.A: Secrets Manager rotates RDS for MySQL credentials on a schedule and can replicate secrets to other Regions, so this meets the need with little effort.
x.B: Parameter Store SecureString parameters have no native scheduled rotation and no multi-Region secret replication.
x.C: Storing credentials in S3 and writing your own Lambda rotation means building and maintaining all of the rotation logic.
x.D: A KMS multi-Region key with DynamoDB global tables and custom Lambda code requires a lot of custom work to do what Secrets Manager provides built in.

x.A: Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics, not a transactional MySQL replacement, and a single node is neither scalable nor highly available.
x.B: A Single-AZ RDS deployment is not highly available, and adding reader instances manually does not automatically scale to unpredictable read demand.
x.C: Aurora is MySQL compatible, a Multi-AZ deployment gives high availability, and Aurora Auto Scaling adds or removes Aurora Replicas as read load changes.
x.D: ElastiCache for Memcached is a cache, not a database, and running it on Spot Instances is not reliable.

x.A: GuardDuty detects threats by analyzing logs, but it does not inspect or filter traffic in the VPC.
x.B: Traffic Mirroring only copies traffic to a target for analysis. It does not filter or block anything.
x.C: AWS Network Firewall is a managed stateful firewall with intrusion prevention. You write custom rules to inspect and filter traffic entering and leaving the VPC, like the on-premises inspection server.
x.D: Firewall Manager centrally manages rules across accounts, but it does not itself perform inspection or filtering.

x.A: QuickSight can connect to both sources, but its dashboards are shared with QuickSight users and groups, not with IAM roles.
x.B: QuickSight connects to both S3 and RDS for PostgreSQL, and you publish dashboards and share them with the management group (full access) and other users or groups (limited access).
x.C: Glue and ETL reports stored in S3 give no data visualization, and S3 bucket policies are too coarse to control dashboard access.
x.D: Athena Federated Query can reach both sources, but reports written to S3 are not visualizations, and bucket policies don't give dashboard-level access.

x.A: An IAM role attached to the instances through an instance profile provides temporary credentials automatically, so the application can access the bucket securely.
x.B: A policy by itself cannot be attached to an EC2 instance. It must be attached to a role, user, or group.
x.C: An IAM group is a set of users and cannot be attached to an instance.
x.D: A user cannot be attached to an instance, and long-term access keys on instances are an insecure practice.

x.A: Sending S3 upload notifications to an SQS queue creates a durable buffer between the upload and the processing, and it keeps no state in the processing code.
x.B: Using the queue as the Lambda event source makes processing automatic, and deleting the message only after success means failures are retried. Together with A this is durable and stateless.
x.C: Lambda cannot monitor a bucket by itself, and keeping a list in memory is not durable because the memory is lost between invocations.
x.D: An EC2 instance that watches the queue and logs to a local text file is neither stateless nor durable, and it adds servers to manage.
x.E: An alert email to a person is not automatic processing, so images would not be compressed without manual work.

x.A: An NLB is not a transparent way to insert a third-party appliance into the traffic path. It forwards to targets and does not preserve the original packets for inspection.
x.B: An ALB works at layer 7 for HTTP and terminates connections, so it cannot pass raw IP packets to a firewall appliance.
x.C: A transit gateway routes between networks but does not inspect packets. You would still need something to steer traffic to the appliance.
x.D: Gateway Load Balancer is built to insert third-party virtual appliances. Traffic reaches the appliance through a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint and returns, with the least operational overhead.

x.A: Instance store volumes cannot be restored from EBS snapshots, so this is not possible.
x.B: Multi-Attach would attach the production volumes themselves to the test instances, so changes in test could affect production.
x.C: Restoring from a snapshot normally loads blocks lazily, so reads on a new volume are slow at first. Creating a new volume first does not remove that initialization delay.
x.D: Fast snapshot restore makes volumes created from the snapshot fully initialized immediately, giving consistently high I/O. Restoring to new volumes keeps test changes separate from production.

x.A: A static-only website cannot process dynamic orders, and S3 is not a transactional store for order data.
x.B: Auto Scaling EC2 behind two ALBs with RDS can work, but you must manage capacity, patching, and database scaling, so it is high overhead.
x.C: EKS with the Cluster Autoscaler means running and maintaining a Kubernetes cluster, which is a lot of overhead, and RDS may struggle with bursts.
x.D: S3 with CloudFront serves static content globally, and API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB scale automatically with millisecond latency. It is fully serverless with the least overhead.

x.A: S3 Standard is multi-AZ but charges the highest storage price even for files that are rarely accessed.
x.B: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between tiers automatically based on access, with no retrieval fees, which fits unpredictable access. It stores data across multiple AZs.
x.C: Standard-IA is multi-AZ but has retrieval fees, which add up when access patterns are unpredictable.
x.D: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so data is lost if that AZ fails.

x.A: Intelligent-Tiering adds a monitoring fee per object and keeps data in more expensive tiers than needed when the data will not be read again.
x.B: After one month the files are not accessed but must be kept, so a lifecycle rule to Glacier Deep Archive gives the lowest storage cost.
x.C: Standard-IA is much more expensive per GB than Deep Archive for data that is never read.
x.D: One Zone-IA is also costlier than Deep Archive and stores in a single AZ, which is risky for backups.

x.A: AWS Budgets is for setting budget thresholds and alerts, not for in-depth cost graphs by instance type.
x.B: Cost Explorer has built-in graphs and filters. You can pick the last two months and group by instance type with no setup, so it gives the answer with the least effort.
x.C: The Billing dashboard shows high-level cost graphs and does not offer the granular filtering needed to find the cause.
x.D: Cost and Usage Reports plus QuickSight can do it, but it takes a lot of setup compared with using Cost Explorer.

x.A: Rewriting as Tomcat on EC2 adds heavy development and server management, and it moves away from the scalable serverless design.
x.B: Switching to DynamoDB with DAX means changing the data model and code, and DAX is a read cache that does not help ingestion bursts.
x.C: SNS pushes messages to subscribers without buffering, so bursts still hit the loader function and the database directly.
x.D: An SQS queue between two Lambda functions buffers bursts, so the loader consumes at a controlled rate. This improves scalability with little configuration.

x.A: AWS Config records resource configuration changes and evaluates them against rules, so it can detect unauthorized changes to S3 bucket settings.
x.B: Trusted Advisor gives periodic best-practice recommendations, not continuous tracking of configuration changes.
x.C: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities in EC2, container images, and Lambda, and it does not track S3 bucket configuration.
x.D: Server access logging records requests to the bucket, not changes to its configuration.
